sections.h2: Who bills property tax in Pensacola?
sections.html:
The Escambia County Tax Collector bills Pensacola property tax, and the Escambia County Property Appraiser sets the values behind the bill. Pensacola sits in Florida's panhandle, and a parcel inside the city limits is taxed by several bodies on one bill.

The tax collector's office says it collects for the school board, the Board of County Commissioners, the City of Pensacola, the Town of Century, the Sheriff, the Downtown Improvement Board and the Northwest Florida Water Management District, among others. A house downtown can therefore carry a line the same house in another part of the county does not. Search your address on the tax collector site to see exactly which lines apply to your parcel.

The appraiser's office states plainly that it has no say over budgets or rates. Its job is to find, locate and value property, run exemptions and keep the maps, sales data and old tax rolls. If you disagree with a tax rate, the place to go is the taxing authority, not the appraiser. If you disagree with a value or an exemption decision, start at the appraiser at escpa.org.

sections.h2: What is Pensacola like for a homeowner who needs to sell?
sections.html:
Pensacola is a Gulf Coast city of about 22.67 square miles and 54,312 people at the 2020 count, according to the city's own profile page citing the Census Bureau. That page lists median household income of $72,699 for 2019 to 2023 and 5,334 veterans.

The city was founded in 1559 by Don Tristan de Luna and Spanish settlers, and it calls itself the City of Five Flags. The Naval Air Station, the Blue Angels and Pensacola International Airport shape the local economy and the pool of buyers and renters who arrive with military orders. Pensacola Beach sits on Santa Rosa Island, and Downtown Pensacola holds the historic district and Palafox Street.

For a seller, the layout matters because Beach parcels and downtown parcels sit in different taxing districts. The appraiser's millage page lists the Downtown Improvement Board as its own authority and Pensacola Beach with its own total, so two houses a few miles apart can have different totals on their bills. Pull the parcel record before you price a sale.

sections.h2: When are Pensacola property tax bills due and what discounts apply?
sections.html:
Bills arrive in November, and Florida allows a discount for early payment: 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February. Unpaid taxes turn delinquent on April 1, and tax certificates are sold by June 1.

The Escambia tax collector's page on Amendment 3 prints the 2026 version of that schedule: 4 percent through December 2, 2026, then 3 percent for the rest of December, 2 percent in January 2027 and 1 percent in February 2027. It adds that the full amount is due in March 2027 and delinquent on April 1, 2027. The same page says voters approved Amendment 3 on November 3, 2026, that it does not change the 2026 bill, and that homestead exemption changes start with the 2027 tax year.

Escambia also runs a quarterly installment plan for taxpayers whose prior year taxes exceeded $100 and who have no escrow account. Applications are due by April 30 of the year you want to start. The schedule is below.

Escambia County installment plan, as printed by the tax collector
InstallmentDueDiscount
FirstJune 306%
SecondSeptember 304.5%
ThirdDecember 313%
FourthMarch 31None

Missing the first payment ends your eligibility for that year, and you then get a regular November bill. The first two installments are based on one quarter of the prior year's taxes, and the last two split the remaining actual liability. The office may also accept partial payments toward current taxes at its discretion, with no discount, and not after March 31.

sections.h2: What exemptions can a Pensacola homeowner claim?
sections.html:
The main one is the homestead exemption, and the appraiser needs your application before March 1 of that tax year. You qualify if you hold title, live in the home and make it your permanent residence on January 1.

  • Homestead: $25,000 on all levies, plus up to $25,000 more on assessed value above $50,000 for levies other than school district taxes.
  • Over 65 additional exemption: available if you are 65 by January 1 and household adjusted gross income is within the cap, which the appraiser prints as $38,686 for 2026. The county exemption is $50,000 and applies only to county taxes. The City of Pensacola exemption is $50,000 and applies only to city taxes.
  • Widow or widower: $5,000, with a death certificate.
  • Disability: $5,000 for total and permanent disability or blindness, with proof from Social Security or a Florida physician.
  • Veterans: $5,000 for a service-connected disability of 10 percent or more, and a full homestead exemption for total and permanent service-connected disability.

The Save Our Homes cap limits yearly growth in a homestead's taxable value to the lower of 3 percent or the change in the Consumer Price Index. The appraiser notes the protection ends when the home is sold, rented or changes ownership. A buyer must apply for the exemption in their own name.

sections.h2: Who pays the Pensacola tax bill in the year of a sale?
sections.html:
Tax for the year of sale is usually settled at closing, and the title company handles it. Ask the title agent for a payoff figure for the parcel and confirm which bills are paid, due or delinquent.

Ask the title agent how the current year gets divided with the buyer. If a prior year is delinquent, a tax certificate may already have been sold on it. Get the current balance from the collector's office before you sign anything. Sellers who have owned the home as a homestead should also ask about portability: the Save Our Homes benefit can transfer to a new Florida homestead established within a limited window, and the appraiser describes the transfer as capped at $500,000.

A sale is also a change of ownership. The assessment resets to market value, so the buyer's first bill can be much higher than yours. That is a reason to price your own carrying costs honestly, and to tell a buyer to look at the appraiser's estimate rather than your old bill.

  • Request a payoff or tax certificate search from the tax collector.
  • Look up the deed history in the clerk's Official Records.
  • Ask the appraiser whether any exemption or classification you hold needs to be cancelled.

sections.h2: Who records the deed in Pensacola?
sections.html:
The Escambia clerk of court keeps the Official Records, and the clerk's office page lists the search at escambiaclerk.com. Florida charges documentary stamp tax on deeds at 70 cents per $100 of consideration in every county except Miami-Dade, collected by the clerk at recording, and all parties to the document are liable for it.

The clerk records the deed, and the appraiser then updates ownership. A change in the owner's name does not move a homestead exemption to the new owner. New owners need to file their own application.

faqs.q: Does the city or the county send the Pensacola bill?
faqs.a: The Escambia County Tax Collector bills it. The City of Pensacola is one of several taxing authorities on the bill, alongside the county, the school district and special districts such as the Downtown Improvement Board.

faqs.q: What is the early payment discount in Pensacola?
faqs.a: It is 4 percent for payment in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February. For 2026 bills, the Escambia tax collector prints 4 percent through December 2, 2026, and delinquency on April 1, 2027.

faqs.q: Can I pay Pensacola property tax in installments?
faqs.a: Yes, if prior year taxes exceeded $100 and you have no escrow account. Apply by April 30 for the year you want to join, with payments due June 30, September 30, December 31 and March 31.

faqs.q: How much is the over 65 exemption in Pensacola?
faqs.a: It is $50,000 against county taxes and a separate $50,000 against City of Pensacola taxes, for owners past 65 whose income sits under the cap. The appraiser prints the 2026 cap as $38,686, with applications closing March 1.

faqs.q: Will a Pensacola sale change the taxable value?
faqs.a: Yes. A sale is a change of ownership, so the property is reassessed at market value and the Save Our Homes cap starts over once the new owner qualifies for homestead. The new owner must apply for the exemption themselves.
